title: From closet servers to a home lab

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Cloud bills can push you to do something unusual: build your own data center in a closet. That's how Antoine's home lab got started.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A real server closet? At home?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. University courses covered IP, VPNs and routing on paper, but running real services at home made it concrete. He wanted a place to experiment without an invoice, and a story to tell that goes beyond using AWS once.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: With Docker. He matched free container stacks to jobs he was paying for in the cloud, like media and dashboards. The rule that stuck was one compose file per concern, so if Plex acted up, he recycled one volume instead of rebuilding the machine.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A Dell PowerEdge R710 with two Xeon processors and 24 gigabytes of RAM, plus an older machine. Bash scripts install Ubuntu, CentOS or Proxmox, so reinstalling after an experiment is painless. Proxmox lets him snapshot before trying something bold.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Like saving a video game before the boss fight.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ha, exactly. For reaching things from outside, Caddy is the reverse proxy, and it gets HTTPS certificates automatically. WireGuard is the V P N, and Antoine contributed small setup helpers so friends could connect without a week of reading manuals.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Did the setup grow over time?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: After a move, he added VLANs and Proxmox virtual machines for club projects, drew the network in Lucidchart and in a C4 style for explaining it, and moved public sites to static hosting, keeping the lab for private services.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A home lab is a sandbox for platform instincts: automate installs, document the layout, and plan for failure. It leads straight to his MediaBox Docker Compose project.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The full post has photos of the real wall of cables.
